content: Malic acid is an organic dicarboxylic acid with a tart taste, commonly found in sour or tart foods. Its salts and esters are referred to as malates. The malate anion serves as an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, alongside fumarate. Additionally, malate can be synthesized from pyruvate through anaplerotic reactions. Malic acid was first isolated from apple juice in 1785 by Carl Wilhelm Scheele. In 1787, Antoine Lavoisier proposed the name acide malique, derived from the Latin word for apple, malum. In biochemistry, malate is a significant compound. In biological systems, malic acid exists exclusively as the (-)-malic acid enantiomer, which is homochiral. During the C4 carbon fixation process, malate acts as a source of carbon dioxide for the Calvin cycle. In the citric acid cycle, (S)-malate is formed by the addition of a hydroxyl group to the si face of fumarate. It can also be generated from pyruvate via anaplerotic reactions. The enzyme malate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reversible conversion of malate to oxaloacetate, utilizing NAD as a cofactor. In plants, malate is produced from starch in the guard cells of leaves. An accumulation of malate reduces water potential, causing water to flow into the guard cells, which leads to the opening of stomata. However, this process does not always result in stomatal opening. Malic acid is present in apples and contributes to the sourness of green apples. In winemaking, malic acid imparts a tart flavor to wine, although its concentration decreases as the fruit ripens. The malolactic fermentation process converts malic acid into the milder lactic acid. As a food additive, malic acid is identified by the E number E296. It is responsible for the intense tartness in extreme candy products, such as Mega Warheads. It is also used in sour candies like Jolly Ranchers, SweeTarts, and Jimmy John’s Salt & Vinegar potato chips, either alone or as a substitute for the less sour citric acid. Some of these candies carry warnings about potential mouth irritation from excessive consumption. In the field of chemistry, malic acid played a pivotal role in the discovery of the Walden inversion and the Walden cycle. In this process, (-)-malic acid is first converted into (+)-chlorosuccinic acid through the action of phosphorus pentachloride. Wet silver oxide then transforms the chlorinated compound into (+)-malic acid, which reacts with phosphorus pentachloride to form (-)-chlorosuccinic acid. The cycle is completed when silver oxide converts this compound back into (-)-malic acid.
